tip: 'Cabe señalar' – literally 'it fits to point out'. 'Caber' (to fit) builds formal Spanish's favorite hedge: 'cabe destacar', 'cabe mencionar' = it's worth noting.
'Hace falta' is literally 'it makes a lack'. The needer is an indirect object: 'Le hace falta descansar' = rest is lacking to him. Needs happen TO you in Spanish.
Two hours and still waiting? Spanish uses plain present for ongoing time: 'Llevo dos horas esperando' – literally 'I carry two hours waiting'. No 'have been' needed.
'Quienquiera que' + subjunctive = whoever.
'Quisiera una mesa' softens the ask with past subjunctive – like 'I should like'. Plain 'quiero' isn't rude, just blunt – 'quisiera' adds the 'could I...?' courtesy.
English brains want 'si tendría' – banned. After 'si' it's past subjunctive: 'Si tuviera vacaciones'. The conditional ('visitaría') lives only in the result half.
'Se hablan' could in theory mean 'they each talk to themselves' – Spanish uses one 'se' for reflexive and reciprocal. The nightly call makes it mutual; 'el uno al otro' would force 'each other'.
You can't 'ask someone to do' in Spanish – no infinitive allowed. 'Pedir' forces a 'que'-clause: 'pedí que me despertaran', literally 'I asked that they wake me'.
'Estará cansado' isn't a prediction – it's a guess. Spanish future tense doubles as 'must be / probably is': he's tired, I bet. Context, not 'will', decides.
'Ojalá' + 'hubiera' + past participle marks an impossible past wish: 'ojalá hubiera aprovechado' = I wish I had made use of it.
'Aunque' + subjunctive ('ofrecieran') means 'even if', a hypothetical – with the indicative it would mean 'although', a plain fact.
'Se' impersonal: no specific subject. 'Se vive bien aquí' = One lives well here / People live well here. Like English 'one' or 'people'.
Passive 'se': the verb agrees with the grammatical subject. 'Se venden camisetas' ('camisetas' = subject, plural → 'venden').
Stuck with the middle seat? 'Me tocó' – 'tocar' means it fell to you by luck of the draw. Lottery wins, chores, and 'el asiento del medio' all just 'te tocan'.
'Se vive' = one lives / people live. Impersonal 'se' with verbs that take no object: 'Se vive bien aquí' = people live well here.
Passive with 'ser' + past participle ('tomada' agrees with 'decisión').
Reported speech: 'conozco' → 'conocía' (present → imperfect) after 'mencionó que'.
'Nuestro/nuestra' agrees with the thing possessed, not the possessor: 'nuestra oficina' (fem.) vs. 'nuestro equipo' (masc.).
Tempted by 'si ganarías'? Never – 'si' refuses the would-form. The hypothesis takes past subjunctive, 'si ganaras la lotería', and 'harías' stays outside the if.
Past choice, present result – mix the halves: 'si hubiera aceptado' (back then) pairs with 'viviría en Madrid' (right now). No rule forces 'hubiera' to match 'habría'.
'Si bien' isn't 'if well' – it's a formal 'although', and no subjunctive follows: 'si bien la casa es pequeña' keeps plain 'es'. It states a fact, not a condition.
'Da a un patio': the room literally 'gives onto' a courtyard. Spanish uses 'dar a' for whatever a window or room faces – no special verb like 'overlooks' needed.
'Cabe' comes from 'caber', to fit: literally 'it fits to highlight that...', there's room for the remark. It powers the formal family: 'cabe mencionar', 'cabe señalar'.
English needs a past tense ('just called'), but Spanish stays in the present: 'acaba de llamar' – roughly 'she finishes-from calling'. The just-happened feel lives in 'acabar de', not the tense.
'Llevo' is literally 'I carry': 'llevo viajando tres semanas' = 'I carry three weeks traveling'. Spanish uses 'llevar' + gerund for ongoing duration – no perfect tense needed.
Why plural 'aceptan'? In passive 'se' the cards are the subject – they 'accept themselves'. The verb agrees with 'tarjetas', not with an invisible 'we'.
'Acabar' normally means 'to finish', but 'acabo de hablar' isn't 'I finish talking' – the 'de' flips it to 'I just spoke'. 'Acabar de' + infinitive timestamps an action; 'acabar' alone ends it.
'Discutir' is a false friend: it usually means to argue, not discuss. 'Se pusieron a discutir' = a heated quarrel, not a debate. Calm discussing is 'hablar de'.
'A la legua' = from a league away, an old road unit about an hour's walk. Spanish measures obviousness as distance: his love shows from miles off.
One trigger, two meanings: 'siempre que tenga' (subjunctive) = if/whenever I ever get the chance – not yet real. With indicative it would just report a habit.
